You compare things and people with the comparative (größer als), equality (so groß wie) and the superlative (am größten, der größte).
Sibiu isn't as noisy as Berlin.
The TV tower is the tallest building in Germany.
My brother is seven years younger than me.
Form the comparative with -er (+ umlaut on short adjectives): größer, älter, wärmer.
Form the superlative: “am …-sten” (after the verb) and “der / die / das …-ste” (before the noun).
Learn the irregular forms: gut – besser – am besten, viel – mehr – am meisten, gern – lieber – am liebsten, hoch – höher, nah – näher.
Describe a city and compare it with yours.
It's Easter. Andrei, Mara's twenty-year-old brother, has come to Berlin for the first time. They're standing on the viewing platform of the TV tower at Alexanderplatz.
Crazy! The view is incredible. How high up are we?
Two hundred and three metres. The TV tower is the tallest building in Germany. It's taller than Cologne Cathedral.
And much taller than the tower in Sibiu! Berlin is so big. You can't see where it ends.
Berlin is about twenty-five times bigger than Sibiu. Almost four million people live here.
So which do you like better? Berlin or Sibiu?
Difficult question. Sibiu is prettier and quieter. The air is better and the mountains are closer. But Berlin is more interesting. There's always something going on here.
Yes, much more expensive. The rent is three times as high as in Sibiu. But I earn more, too.
And the food? Is it as good as at home?
No! Nothing is as good as Mum's cooking. But Lena's cake is the best in Berlin. You'll try it tonight.
Lena… Is she the baker? The one in the photos? She's prettier than in the photos, isn't she?
Andrei! She's nine years older than you!
I only asked! And I'm more mature than most people my age.
groß → größer (“GRØ-ser”, ö like the vowel in “her” with rounded lips), jung → jünger (“YÜNG-er”, ü = “ee” with rounded lips), hoch → höher. You can clearly hear the umlaut!
The superlative ends in “-sten”: am schönsten = “am SHØN-sten”. After -t / -d / -s / -z you add -e-: am ältesten, am heißesten.
Watch the soft “ch”: höchste = “HØ-khste”, nächste = “NAY-khste” (a very soft, breathy sound, like the “h” in “huge”).
A long word: “ZAY-ens-vür-dikh-kite”. Break it into pieces!
You add “-er” to the adjective. To compare two things you use “als” (than):
Many SHORT adjectives (one syllable) with a, o, u take an UMLAUT:
“als” = than (difference). Don't use “wie” for a difference! “Berlin ist größer als Sibiu”, not “größer wie”.
Lena is the same age as Jonas.
Nothing is as good as Mum's cooking.
The rent is three times as high as in Sibiu.
Summary: so … WIE (the same), …er ALS (more / less).
Two forms, depending on where the adjective stands:
Lena's cake is the best in Berlin.
Who is the oldest? — Mrs Hoffmann is the oldest in the building.
After -t, -d, -s, -ß, -z you add -e-: am ältesten, am heißesten, am kürzesten. But: am größten (exception).
I like tea, I prefer coffee, and I like hot chocolate best of all.
“mehr” is never declined: “mehr Geld”, “mehr Menschen”, “mehr Zeit”.
Er ist so größer als ich.
My brother is younger than me.
Wie hoch ist die Miete in Berlin?
Wessen Kuchen ist der beste in Berlin?
Berlin is more expensive than Sibiu.

Andrei stayed in Berlin for five days. Mara had made a plan with the most important sights: the Brandenburg Gate, the Reichstag, the East Side Gallery, Museum Island. But Andrei wasn't the typical tourist.

At the Brandenburg Gate he said: “It's smaller than I thought.” At the Reichstag he liked the glass dome, but the queue in front of it was longer than the dome was tall. At the East Side Gallery he didn't photograph the famous paintings, but an old man who was playing the accordion there.
Andrei, you're the most difficult tourist in the world. What do you like most about Berlin?
Honestly? Your building. Your neighbours. This old man with the tram lamp is cooler than any museum.

That was true. Andrei had made friends with Ludwig straight away. On the first evening they sat together until midnight, Ludwig with his guitar, Andrei with his, because Andrei played too. He even played better than Ludwig, which Ludwig admitted after the third beer. “But I play older,” he said. “That counts for something too.”

Ludwig told Andrei about his band, about Ingrid, about that night in November 1989. Andrei told Ludwig about Sibiu, about their father's bees, which in summer made the best honey in the whole of Transylvania, and about his studies: he was studying computer science, but actually he'd rather have done music. “I know that feeling,” said Ludwig. “I'd rather have become a guitarist than a tram driver too. But you know what? You can be both. By day you drive the tram, in the evening you play the guitar. Life is longer than you think.”

On the second day, Andrei helped at the bakery. At four in the morning. Voluntarily. Mara couldn't believe it, because at home Andrei never got up before ten. Lena showed him how to shape pretzels. His first ten pretzels looked like snakes, the next ten like hearts, and the last ten were almost as beautiful as Lena's.
You learn faster than Emre. And Emre has been working here for three years!
I've got a good teacher. The best in Berlin, my sister says.
Mara, who was just about to get a coffee, stopped in the doorway. Lena blushed. Lena never blushed. Mara turned around slowly and went back upstairs. Some things are better left unseen.

In the afternoon, Andrei asked his sister, casually, whether Lena had a boyfriend. Mara said: “Ask her yourself.” Andrei said: “That's harder than any university exam.” Mara laughed and said nothing more. Younger brothers are sometimes cleverer than you think, but not always braver.

On the third day it rained. It was colder than in Sibiu, and the wind was stronger. Andrei, Mara and Lena took the S-Bahn to the Wannsee. There was nobody on the beach, just a few ducks and a man with a dog that was even smaller than Fritz. They sat under a roof in an empty café and drank the hottest cocoa in the world.
Is Sibiu really prettier than Berlin? Mara always says so.

Sibiu is smaller, older, quieter. The houses have eyes, little windows in the roof that look at you. And the mountains are so close that in the morning you can see them from your bed. You have to come. It's most beautiful in summer.

Lena looked out of the window at the grey rain. “Maybe,” she said. “Maybe in August. The bakery is closed for two weeks then.” Mara drank her cocoa and said nothing. But under the table she sent her mother a message: “Mum, I think we're getting visitors in August.”

On the last evening there was a farewell dinner at Ludwig's. Mrs Hoffmann sent down a bottle of wine, “the oldest one I have”, with a note. Ludwig and Andrei played a Romanian song together that Andrei had taught him, and Ludwig sang the chorus in Romanian, with an accent funnier than any joke.

On the fourth day, Mara took her brother with her to the hospital, because he wanted to see where she worked. Jonas showed him the ward and told him that Mara was the fastest nurse on ward 4, but also the most patient. Mr Schulz, who was there again for a check-up, said in Berlin dialect: “Your sister is the best, young man. The best of all!” Andrei didn't understand a word, but he understood everything.

At the airport, Andrei gave his sister a long hug. Then he said: “You know, I was afraid you were lonely here. That Berlin was too big, too cold, too rushed. But you have more family here than some people have at home.”
And which was your best day in Berlin?
Andrei thought about it. Then he smiled: “The day with the pretzels. At four in the morning. But I won't tell Mum that. Otherwise she won't believe it was me.”
